transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-11-13
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Oliver Park (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Ortiz (Pacifica CTO), Rajiv Malik (Lead ML Eng), Sara Kim (Platform Eng), Tom Baxter (Procurement)

Auto-generated summary (may be noisy):
- Pacifica evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for chat summarization and claims triage.
- Primary constraints: p95 latency targets for streaming summaries (goal ~400ms p95 for 256-512 token responses), concurrency ~200-500 simultaneous chats, strict HIPAA/data residency, SSO/SAML, KMS integration.
- Redwood to provide benchmark spreadsheet, initial dedicated sizing, and schedule deeper private deploy session.

Topics:
- p95 targets and what they mean for streaming vs non-streaming flows
- batching, prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs
- dedicated capacity sizing and autoscale burst behavior
- private deployment network egress and KMS/SSO integration

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll run about 45 minutes. quick round intro, then dive into your latency and throughput needs.
[00:28] Dr. Lena Ortiz: hi, lena here. we run a clinical triage assistant and a patient-facing summarizer. main ask is consistent p95 for streaming responses, patients get partial transcriptions. we need predictability.
[00:59] Rajiv Malik: yea and hi i'm rajiv. our throughput spikes a lot, e.g. marketing campaigns, could be 300 to 700 concurrent streams for short bursts; typical baseline 120. critical is p95 under 500ms end-to-end for 256 token flows.
[01:35] Oliver Park: quick clarifying q — when you say 500ms p95 is that server-to-server or end-to-end including client pre/post processing?
[01:48] Rajiv Malik: that's end-to-end as measured by our app, so includes transport on our side but we want the inference portion to be sub-350ms ideally for 256 tokens.
[02:12] Maya Chen: okay good, that maps to two levers: pick hosting mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private) and runtime config (batch size, model quant, KV cache). we'll walk through tradeoffs.
[02:41] Tom Baxter: quick procurement note — we need to understand cost delta between hosted usage and a reserved dedicated contract. our compliance team also prefers private control plane if cost isn't insane.
[03:05] Sara Kim: also HIPAA requirement, data residency in US-West, and KMS integration. SAML SSO for our engineers.
[03:28] Oliver Park: we support SAML/SSO, and Redwood Private offers a customer-controlled control plane with KMS/HSM support — though on-prem comes with more ops overhead.
[03:52] Dr. Lena Ortiz: how does p95 change between hosted and dedicated? we've seen other vendors quote best-case latencies but then big variance.
[04:10] Oliver Park: good question. hosted can be fastest for cold-start-friendly streaming because we run optimized pools, but dedicated gives you more predictable tail because you own the GPU pool. hosted has auto-fallbacks and multi-variant routing which smooths out transient spikes. in practice for streaming with prefix caching, dedicated can hit slightly lower variance if you provision steady capacity.
[04:44] Rajiv Malik: are there numbers you can share for p95 on typical open models? say 7B-13B variants with streaming enabled for 256 tokens.
[05:01] Maya Chen: absolutely — we'll share a benchmark sheet. rough off-the-cuff: with continuous batching and KV cache hit-rate ~60%, you'll often see inference latencies in hosted optimized pools around 200–300ms p95 for 256 tokens on the 13B quantized profiles; dedicated similar or slightly better if you size for steady-state. but worst-case cold starts or cache-miss scenarios can spike.
[05:35] Speaker 2: mm-hmm (inaudible)
[05:45] Rajiv Malik: ok can you explain cache hit-rate and how to get high hit-rate? we have a lot of repeated system prompts but unique user messages.
[06:05] Oliver Park: sure — Redwood supports prefix / KV caching so repeated system-level context or earlier conversation prefixes get cached. that reduces per-token compute because KV cache avoids recomputing previous tokens. for chat flows where the system prompt is identical across sessions, hit-rate can be very high. other strategies: use shorter system prompts, bump caching TTL, and use model sharding for common contexts.
[06:36] Sara Kim: what about batch vs streaming tradeoffs — our product needs token-by-token streaming to the client to improve perceived latency. batching seems at odds with streaming.
[06:52] Oliver Park: correct tension. continuous batching groups concurrent requests and improves GPU utilization — but for token-level streaming you can still batch at micro-batch sizes and use early token flushes. Redwood's runtime supports micro-batching for streaming so you get some cost savings without adding big latency. we'll show numbers in the sheet.
[07:22] Dr. Lena Ortiz: what about quantization? we don't want hallucination risk to increase.
[07:35] Maya Chen: quantization lowers memory and can reduce cost and sometimes latency. RedwoodOptimize recommends quant profiles per workload. for summarization tasks we often use 4-bit quant with careful calibration; our quality monitoring would flag regressions so you can A/B test.
[07:58] Rajiv Malik: can you do a short example: suppose 300 concurrent streams, average response 300 tokens, p95 target 400ms — what is the rough infra footprint?
[08:16] Oliver Park: rough back-of-the-envelope: a 13B quantized model with efficient attention and micro-batching can sustain — depending on GPU type — roughly 20–40 streaming streams per GPU steady-state for moderate token lengths. so 300 concurrent steady would map to 8–15 GPUs plus buffer for burst; dedicated autoscale handles short bursts but reserved pool of ~12 GPUs is plausible. exact numbers depend on token/sec per user and H2O? sorry, the model specifics. we'll size precisely after you share token histogram.
[09:05] Rajiv Malik: cool. and pricing? quick delta hosted vs dedicated?
[09:15] Maya Chen: hosted is usage-based — per-token and per-embedding units. dedicated is reserved capacity with fixed monthly commit and lower unit costs at scale. example: at 300 concurrent long-run, dedicated often becomes cheaper if sustained load because you amortize GPU cost; hosted is better for spiky unpredictable loads. we'll produce scenarios in the cost spreadsheet.
[09:42] Tom Baxter: for procurement we need SLAs — do you have p95 SLA for hosted?
[09:50] Maya Chen: we publish performance profiles but SLA-backed p95 is typically part of Dedicated/Enterprise contracts. Hosted has best-effort plus uptime SLA; Dedicated offers tailored latency SLOs in contract.
[10:12] Sara Kim: network egress and data flow for private deployment — can we retain logs in our VPC?
[10:24] Oliver Park: yes Private keeps control plane inside your VPC, logs can be shipped to your storage, and you maintain key control with KMS/HSM. that covers HIPAA concerns.
[10:42] Dr. Lena Ortiz: any major gotchas with onboarding private? timeline?
[10:51] Maya Chen: private deployment onboarding typically 6–10 weeks for VPC-based control plane, depends on customer's infra team bandwidth. on-prem air-gapped will be longer. we also run initial benchmark tests to validate p95.
[11:12] Rajiv Malik: can we run a small POC in hosted, then lift to dedicated/private if results look good?
[11:22] Maya Chen: yes, that's common. start with hosted for quick bench, move to dedicated for steady-state and then private if you need full control. our rollout tooling lets you pin model versions and fallback policies during migration.
[11:40] Speaker 3: (crosstalk)
[11:48] Rajiv Malik: about cold starts — how do sudden spikes affect p95?
[11:57] Oliver Park: spikes can cause queueing or spin-up latency. hosted uses multi-region pools and warm warmers to reduce cold start incidence. Dedicated can be kept warm, but you pay for idle capacity. Redwood also supports burst capacity: you keep base reserved and allow ephemeral hosted burst — hybrid approach.
[12:24] Sara Kim: any encryption in transit to our VPC?
[12:30] Oliver Park: yes TLS for all traffic; for private you can use private peering and mTLS.
[12:40] Dr. Lena Ortiz: what about auditing and traceability for clinicians?
[12:48] Maya Chen: we offer token-level tracing, per-route dashboards, and audit logs export. you can tie logs to your identity provider for auditing.
[13:05] Rajiv Malik: ok let's talk measurement: how do you measure p95 for streaming where partial tokens arrive earlier?
[13:20] Oliver Park: two approaches: measure latency to first token and measure time to complete generation. For p95 of perceived latency, teams often use time-to-first-byte (TTFB) for streaming. For end-to-end response p95 you measure completion. We'll recommend specific metrics in the sheet.
[13:46] Dr. Lena Ortiz: good to call that out, our clinicians care about first seen content not full doc.
[13:55] Maya Chen: noted. we'll include TTFB targets and examples.
[14:05] Tom Baxter: procurement question — any discounts for multi-region dedicated reserved?
[14:13] Maya Chen: yes enterprise contracts can include multi-region capacity and volume discounts; we'll outline in the proposal.
[14:25] Rajiv Malik: any customers in health you can reference re: HIPAA?
[14:31] Maya Chen: we have healthcare references, yes — we'll share names under NDA.
[14:40] Oliver Park: quick technical aside: KV cache eviction policy can affect tail latency under long sessions — if you have very long conversational histories, we'd recommend periodic summarization to bound context length.
[15:05] Rajiv Malik: that maps to our design, we keep rolling summary at 2k tokens.
[15:12] Speaker 1: OK
[15:20] Maya Chen: next I'll quickly map out the immediate playbook: 1) you send prompt corpus + QPS histogram; 2) we run hosted benchmark using your prompts; 3) SE deep-dive for private/dedicated sizing; 4) proposal with cost scenarios.
[15:44] Dr. Lena Ortiz: timeline — we'd like a 2-week rapid benchmark and then decision on pilot by end of month.
[15:53] Maya Chen: that seems doable. we'll aim to deliver the benchmark CSV within 10 business days.
[16:05] Rajiv Malik: one last nit — how do you handle model updates and version pinning?
[16:14] Oliver Park: model pinning is supported; rollouts can be canary, A/B, or instant. we also provide eval hooks and regression alerts tied to prompt sets.
[16:30] Sara Kim: security sign-off will want SOC2 Type II evidence and penetration test summary.
[16:40] Maya Chen: got it — we'll attach SOC2 report and recent pentest summary in the follow-up.
[16:50] Tom Baxter: who will own contract review? me and legal — we'll need standard data processing addendum for HIPAA.
[16:59] Maya Chen: noted, Tom. we'll include DPA + BAA language options in proposal.
[17:10] Dr. Lena Ortiz: any risks with quantization for clinical summarization?
[17:18] Oliver Park: quality regressions are possible; RedwoodOptimize flags regressions and we recommend benchmark A/B with golden set. if regen risk is unacceptable, you can stick to higher-precision profiles.
[17:38] Maya Chen: wrapping up — action items we've captured. competitors you mentioned include Anthropic and in-house; we'll benchmark against a couple of public profiles and include those comparisons.
[18:00] Rajiv Malik: good. also can you show an example spreadsheet row for expected cost per 1M tokens in hosted vs dedicated?
[18:09] Maya Chen: yes will include sample scenarios: baseline, sustained, and burst.
[18:20] Dr. Lena Ortiz: thanks all. when do we schedule the SE deep-dive? week of 11/26 works for us.
[18:28] Maya Chen: I'll follow up with a calendar invite and attach the benchmark sheet.
[18:36] Oliver Park: i'll prepare dedicated sizing and a short checklist for the private deploy requirements.
[18:45] Tom Baxter: thanks everyone.
[18:50] Maya Chen: thanks — we'll share materials and next steps. end call.
